    International Journal of Mechanical Sciences

    Volume 256, 15 October 2023, 108509

    Sensible multiscale symbol dynamic entropy for fault diagnosis of bearing

    Author links open overlay panel, , , , ,
    https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ijmecsci.2023.108509Get rights and content

    Highlights

    • •

      A novel fault diagnosis method based on SMSDE is proposed.

    • •

      The slippage-averaging multiscale approach is used to enhance the SMSDE.

    • •

      The proposed SMSDE is used to extract multiscale features of mechanical faults.

    • •

      SMSDE can more accurately describe small fluctuations in vibration signals.

    • •

      The effectiveness of the proposed method is verified by three experimental cases.

    Abstract

    Due to the complex service conditions of rolling bearings, vibration signals arising therefrom exhibit non-linear characteristics, which means that single-scale feature extraction techniques cannot extract fault features. Multiscale symbolic dynamic entropy (MSDE) is a new technique that has recently emerged and been applied to fault diagnosis in machinery. However, MSDE has limitations such as its poor stability, large errors, and even loss of information. To this end, a novel sensible multiscale symbol dynamic entropy (SMSDE) method was proposed. For SMSDE, the signal was first decomposed using empirical mode decomposition, and then the useful intrinsic mode functions were selected for reconstruction to decrease noise. Secondly, the slippage-averaging multiscale approach was designed to coarse-grain the signal, which considers the connection of data before and after the breakpoint, thus reducing the error. The method can not only decrease noise, but also avoid the loss of key information, thereby extracting sensitive feature information. The results with multiple synthesized signals show that the proposed method is more robust than the other eight entropy methods. Furthermore, the real bearing signals of the three cases indicate that compared with other advanced entropy methods, SMSDE can better distinguish the various states of the bearing.

    1. Introduction

    Rolling bearings are key components of machines and have been widely used in various major industries such as the railway, automotive, aerospace, and chemical industries [1,2]. However, rolling bearings are often subject to service in a variety of complex and harsh environments, which inevitably lead to various faults. If these faults are not dealt with timeously, the service life of the machine will be reduced, which in turn will generate economic losses and cause accidents [3]. Therefore, bearing fault diagnosis is essential to maintain the safety and reliability of the machine [4].

    During service, the vibration signal of the bearing has strong non-linearity, and the complexity of the signal when in the presence of a defect is difficult to detect by using conventional time-frequency analysis methods [5,6]. Entropy is a method to describe the complexity of time series and has been applied to machine fault diagnosis [7], [8], [9], [10]: this can take several forms: permutation entropy [11], sample entropy [12], and fuzzy entropy [13]. Nevertheless, the aforementioned entropy method entails only single-scale analysis of the signal and cannot provide in-depth information about the complexity of the signal. To overcome the limitations of single-scale entropy, Costa et al. [14] developed a multiscale entropy technique. Thereafter, methods based on multiscale entropy were applied to the field of fault diagnosis [15,16]. For example, Verma et al. [17] developed a fault diagnosis method based on multiscale sample entropy (MSE) and gray relational analysis. To overcome the shortcomings of traditional multiscale entropy, Zhao et al. [18] proposed a fault diagnosis method based on improved MSE. Wang et al. [19] proposed a novel refined composite multiscale sample entropy (RCMSE) to extract features and improve the accuracy of fault diagnosis. In addition, some improved MSE algorithms have been applied to machine fault diagnosis [20], [21], [22], [23]. Unlike MSE, the theory of multiscale permutation entropy (MPE) is relatively simple [24,25], involving few parameters and rapid computation [26,27]. For example, Ye et al. [28] proposed a method of MPE and linear local tangent space alignment, which successfully identified multiple fault states. To extract fault features from a noisy signal, Minhas et al. [29] proposed an improved MPE method that first decomposes the signal using complementary ensemble empirical mode decomposition. To increase the accuracy of bearing fault diagnosis, Zheng et al. [30] designed a method based on MPE and Laplacian score. Furthermore, multiscale fuzzy entropy (MFE) incorporates fuzzy set theory into the calculation process to reduce the error of the entropy value [31], [32], [33]. For example, to detect bearing faults timeously, then determine the location of the defect, Zheng et al. [34] proposed a novel composite MFE. Chen et al. [35] designed a feature extraction method called improved MFE and combined it with topological learning and out-of-sample embedding. To extract the features efficiently, a refined composite multiscale fuzzy entropy (RCMFE) was proposed [36] and validated on several experimental signals; other studies have also applied MFE to fault diagnosis in rotating machinery [37], [38], [39].

    Nevertheless, the aforementioned MSE and RCMSE are highly dependent on the time series, and the calculated results are unstable and prone to error [40,41]. Additionally, MPE does not fully consider the relationship between signal amplitudes, leading to a loss of statistical information [42,43]. Furthermore, MFE and RCMFE have long computation times and low efficiency [44], which cannot meet the on-line monitoring requirements of industrial production [45,46]. To address these issues, Li et al. [47] proposed the multiscale symbolic dynamic entropy (MSDE) technique, which has exhibited good performance in terms of computational efficiency and stability. Currently, MSDE has been applied to mechanical fault diagnosis [48,49]. For example, Liu et al. [50] proposed an improved MSDE and verified its effectiveness in experiments with different noise signals. Li et al. [51] proposed a new bearing fault diagnosis method based on composite multiscale symbolic dynamic entropy (CMSDE). To extract the fault features of the bearing signals, Yang et al. [52] proposed a novel refined composite multiscale symbolic dynamic entropy (RCMSDE). However, the algorithms of MSDE and its variants still use the conventional multiscale approach to process the signal to be analyzed, leading to a loss of information. Furthermore, when the scale factor increases, the aforementioned method suffers increasing error and decreasing stability. Additionally, the complex working environment around mechanical equipment causes the vibration signals collected to contain meaningless components (noise). To this end, a new sensible multiscale symbol dynamic entropy (SMSDE) was proposed in the present study. For SMSDE, the vibration signal was first decomposed using empirical mode decomposition (EMD) [53,54], and the useful intrinsic mode function (IMF) was selected for reconstruction to decrease the amount of noise. Secondly, the slippage-averaging multiscale approach was designed to replace the conventional multiscale approach, which considers the connection between data before and after breakpoints, thus reducing errors. Therefore, the method not only decreases the contribution arising from meaningless signal components, but also avoids the loss of key information, overcoming the limitations of the conventional multiscale approach. Ultimately, the SMSDE was used to extract sensitive fault features, and the features were fed into the support vector machines (SVM) [55,56] for pattern recognition to achieve bearing fault diagnosis. The key contributions of this study are described as follows:

    • (1)

      The slippage-averaging multiscale approach is designed, considering the connection between data before and after the breakpoint, thus avoiding the loss of key information and reducing errors;

    • (2)

      SMSDE integrates the merits of IMF reconstruction and the slippage-averaging multiscale approach, which not only reduce noise but also mine key signal information, thus extracting sensitive features;

    • (3)

      The results of three bearing experimental cases show that the proposed SMSDE can extract fault features with higher accuracy and robustness.

    The remainder of this article is organized as follows: Section 2 presents the methodology of SMSDE, including its theoretical derivation as well as the validation of the synthesized signal. The proposed fault diagnosis method is covered in Section 3. Section 4 shows the analysis and verification results of the three bearing experiments; Section 5 concludes.

    2. The proposed sensible multiscale symbol dynamic entropy method

    In this section, we will introduce the proposed SMSDE fault diagnosis method. Firstly, we present the theory of SDE and the theory of MSDE in Sections 2.1 and 2.2, respectively. Secondly, the theory of SMSDE is introduced in Section 2.3, and its IMF reconstruction and the slippage-averaging multiscale approach process are shown in Fig. 3. Finally, the performance of the proposed SMSDE is verified by multiple synthesized signals in Section 2.4.

    2.1. Theory of symbol dynamic entropy

    We will introduce the theory of SDE in this section. However, SDE is only a single-scale entropy method, which cannot mine the deep information of the signal.

    Assuming X¯={x¯1,x¯2,x¯3,…,x¯n} represents a time series of length N, the main steps of the SDE method are as follows:

    • (1)

      The time series can be converted into a symbolic series. Maximum entropy partitioning has the advantage of adaptive segmentation [57], so it is used to convert time series into symbolic time series. Meanwhile, the symbolic time series is constructed as an embedding vector as follows:(1)Zjm,λ={z(j),z(j+λ),…,z(j+(m−1)λ)},j=1,2,…,N−(m−1)λ,

    where, m denotes the embedding dimension and λ represents the time delay;
    • (1)

      The probability qaμ,m,λ(a=1,2,…,μm) is then calculated for each state pattern as follows:(2)P(qaμ,m,λ)=∥{j:j≤N−(m−1)λ,type(Zjμ,m,λ)=qaμ,m,λ}∥N−(m−1)λ,

    where, ‖.‖ depicts the cardinality of a set, and type(.) represents the map from symbol space to state pattern space;
    • (1)

      The probability qaμ,m,λ of the state pattern is used to construct the state mode matrix[P(q1μ,m,λ),P(q2μ,m,λ),…,P(qmμ,m,λ)]1×μm;

    • (2)

      The probability of state transitions is then calculated as follows:(3)P(σb|qaμ,m,λ)=∥{j:j≤N−mλ,type(Zjμ,m,λ)=qaμ,m,λ,z(j+mλ)=σb}∥N−(m−1)λ,

    where, a = 1, 2, …, μm and b = 1, 2, …, μ. Additionally,μ represents the number of symbols, and μm denotes the number of states;
    • (1)

      P(σb|qaμ,m,λ) is obtained and the state transition matrix is constructed therewith:(4)[P(σ1|q1)P(σ2|q1)⋯P(σμ|q1)P(σ1|q2)P(σ2|q2)⋯P(σμ|q2)⋮⋮⋯⋮P(σ1|qμm)P(σ2|qμm)⋯P(σμ|qμm)].

    • (2)

      According to the theorem of Shannon entropy, the SDE is defined as follows:(5)sde(X¯,μ,m,λ)=−∑a=1μmP(qaμ,m,λ)lnP(qaμ,m,λ)−∑a=1μm∑b=1μP(qaμ,m,λ)ln(P(qaμ,m,λ)P(σb|qaμ,m,λ)).

    • (3)

      Finally, the SDE is normalized so that it conforms to 0<SDE(X¯,μ,m,λ)<1, as follows:(6)SDE(X¯,μ,m,λ)=sde(X¯,μ,m,λ)/ln(μm+1).

    2.2. Theory of multiscale symbol dynamic entropy

    We will present the theory of MSDE in this section. MSDE is able to mine the deep information of the signal from multiple scales, which improves the shortcomings of SDE. However, the MSDE still uses the conventional multiscale approach to process the signal, leading to a loss of information.

    SDE analyses the vibration signals of bearings by single-scale techniques. However, the single-scale entropy value cannot mine deep information conveyed within the signal, leading to difficulties in fault feature extraction. Through the conventional multiscale approach, MSDE can overcome the shortcomings of SDE to a certain extent. The coarse-grained process of MSDE is shown in Fig. 1, and the flowchart describing its algorithm is shown in Fig. 2 (the abbreviations commonly used in this study are listed in Table 1).

    2.3. Theory of sensible multiscale symbol dynamic entropy

    We will present the theory of the proposed SMSDE in this section. SMSDE integrates the merits of IMF reconstruction and the slippage-averaging multiscale approach, which not only reduce noise but also mine key signal information, thus extracting sensitive features.

    There are, nevertheless, some limitations to MSDE: firstly, the coarse-grained process of the MSDE is not performed in a continuous displacement operation, as shown in Fig. 1. Taking the scale factor τ = 3 as an example, the first data point y1(3) of the MSDE coarse-grained time series is obtained after calculating the average value from the original time series sample points (x1,x2andx3); its second data point y2,1(3) is then the average of the sample points (x4,x5andx6), not (x2,x3andx4). Directly skipping the sample points y3,1(3) for calculation, which is equivalent to forming a break thereat, causing sudden changes in the calculated entropy. Secondly, the coarse-grained process of MSDE entails the continuous division of the original time series, and as the scale factor increases, the divided subseries contains smaller data points. However, the decreasing number of subseries data points will reduce the stability of the entropy results and the calculation error will increase.

    To address the shortcomings of MSDE, SMSDE was proposed. For SMSDE, EMD is first used for denoising, and then the useful IMF is selected for reconstruction, to obtain the reconstruction signal. Secondly, based on the slippage-averaging multiscale approach, SMSDE can connect the data before and after the breakpoint, thus avoiding loss of key information. The better to understand SMSDE, the random signal is taken as an example: its IMF reconstruction and the slippage-averaging multiscale approach process are shown in Fig. 3. From Fig. 3, the first data point y1,1(3) of the slippage-averaging multiscale approach is obtained after calculating the average value from the sample points (x1,x2andx3). Subsequently, its second data point y2,1(3) is the average of (x2,x3andx4). Then, the third sample point y3,1(3) is the average of (x3,x4andx5).

    Therefore, to overcome the limitations of MSDE, a new SMSDE is proposed in this study. The main steps of SMSDE are as follows:

    • (1)

      For the original time seriesX¯={x¯1,x¯2,x¯3,…,x¯n}, EMD is applied to eliminate the disturbing noise, thus obtaining the denoised time series, as follows:(7)X=∑i=1edIMFi+r(t),

    where, dIMFi denotes the series of IMFs obtained from the decomposition, e is the number of IMFs, and r(t) represents the residual. After extensive experiments in this study and combined with related research, e = 5 herein;
    • (1)

      The denoised time series X = {x1,x2,x3,…, xn} is processed based on Eq. (8), resulting in a new coarse-grained time series with scale factor τ. From Fig. 4, based on the slippage-averaging multiscale approach, for each scale factor τ, τ new coarse-grained time series zk(τ)(k=1,2,⋯,τ) can be obtained. However, the MSDE only considers a coarse-grained series z1(τ). Thus, the SMSDE method can improve the stability of entropy values at breakpoints compared with conventional multiscale techniques.(8)yk,j(τ)=∑f=0τ−1xf+k+τ(j−1)τ,1≤j≤Nτ,1≤k≤τ.

    • (2)

      The SDE values of each coarse-grained time series zk(τ)(k=1,2,…,τ) at scale factor τ are calculated, and the average of these SDE values is solved based on Eq. (9). Finally, the average value of SDE for each scale factor is taken as a function of the calculated entropy result. Thus, the SMSDE is defined as follows:(9)SMSDE(X,μ,m,λ,τ)=1τ∑kτSDE(zk(τ),μ,m,λ).

    Fig. 5 presents the flowchart through the proposed SMSDE, where τm is the maximum value of the scale factor. For SMSDE, it first eliminates environmental noise at low frequencies, and then calculates the SDE values of all coarse-grained time series and averages them to obtain the final results. Therefore, the proposed SMSDE can not only handle short time series with few data points, but also improve the stability of the computational results.

    2.4. Validation and analysis using synthesized signals

    In this section, the performance of the proposed SMSDE is verified by multiple synthesized signals and compared with eight existing entropy methods (RCMSDE, CMSDE, MSDE, RCMFE, MFE, RCMSE, MSE, and MPE).

    To illustrate the influences of signal length on SMSDE, RCMSDE, and MSDE, white noise and pink noise with lengths of 500, 1500, 2500, 3500, 4500, and 5500 are taken for analysis. White noise (wn) and pink noise (pn) are often used to evaluate the performance of entropy, and their signals are shown in Fig. 6. For SMSDE, the selection of four key parameters (i.e. the symbol number μ, embedding dimension m, time delay λ, and scale factor τ) has different effects on its performance. Firstly, when the symbol number μ = 1, only single-symbol time series will be generated; when the symbol number is too large, it will reduce the efficiency. Secondly, when the embedding dimension m is too small, there will be only a small number of states μm. However, when m is too large, it will increase the computation time. Thus, the symbol number and embedding dimension have a significant effect on the performance of SMSDE. After many repeated experiments and combined with related studies, μ and m were set to 6 and 3, respectively. As with MSE, MPE, and MFE, time delay has little effect on SMSDE, which is generally set to λ = 1. In general, the scale factor is set to τ = 20. For more information on the selection of symbol number, embedding dimension, time delay, and scale factor, please refer to [47,50,51]. Hence, the parameters of SMSDE are μ = 6, m = 3, λ = 1, and τ = 20, respectively. In which, for fair comparison, the parameters of RCMSDE and MSDE match those of SMSDE. As seen in Fig. 7, for a pn signal, the entropy value of SMSDE is more stable compared to RCMSDE and MSDE, and the effect of data length on the entropy value becomes smaller after the length is greater than 3500. For a wn signal, the trends of the entropy curves of SMSDE, RCMSDE, and MSDE are roughly the same, but the fluctuations of RCMSDE and MSDE gradually increase with the scale factor, while the curve of SMSDE remains smooth with almost no fluctuation therein. Therefore, in this study, the length of the data is chosen to be 3500.

    To clarify the performance of the SMSDE method, 35 sets of wn signals and pn signals with a data length of 3500 are taken for analysis and compared with RCMSDE, CMSDE, MSDE, RCMFE, MFE, RCMSE, MSE, and MPE, respectively. The calculated results (mean and standard deviation) arising from the use of different entropy methods for the two noise signals are shown in Fig. 8, where the parameter settings of RCMSDE, CMSDE, and MSDE are the same as those of SMSDE. Then, the parameters of RCMFE and MFE are set to similar tolerance r = 0.25, fuzzy power n = 2, embedding dimension m = 3, time delay λ = 1, and scale factor τ = 20. Additionally, the parameters of RCMSE and MSE are set to similar tolerance r = 0.25, embedding dimension m = 3, time delay λ = 1, and scale factor τ = 20. Furthermore, the parameters of MPE are set to embedding dimension m = 3, time delay λ = 1, and scale factor τ = 20. For detailed information on the selection of parameters for MSE, RCMSE, MPE, MFE, and RCMFE, please refer to [18,19,28,35,36]. From Fig. 8, the trends of the entropy curves of SMSDE, RCMSDE, CMSDE, and MSDE are similar, so can distinguish the two noisy signals. For both signals, the error of SMSDE is smaller than the result of RCMSDE. However, the curves of CMSDE and MSDE for pn signals are not smooth and show slight fluctuations. Additionally, the results of the MFE and MSE calculations not only generate a large error, but the two curves appear to cross each other. Compared with MFE and MSE, the entropy curves of RCMFE and RCMSE are smoother and incur smaller errors. For MPE, although the two curves do not appear to cross, the error is large, and the results are poor. Hence, SMSDE can not only distinguish between the two noise signals, but also incurs a smaller error and exhibits greater stability.

    When the engineering machinery fails, its vibration signal is often a non-stationary AM-FM signal and contains a variety of environmental noise interference sources. To verify the effectiveness of the proposed SMSDE, white noise with different signal noise ratio (SNR) is added to z(t) of Eq. (10) for analysis, and the results are shown in Fig. 9. The synthesized signals of z(1), z(2), z(3), z(4), z(5), and z(6) are obtained by adding SNRs of 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, and 35 dB to z(t), respectively. Additionally, the SNR is defined in Eq. (11).(10)z(t)=[0.8+0.5sin(30πt2)]cos[10πt+sin(300πt2)]+0.1cos(20πt2)sin(2πt),z(1)=z(t)+z(t)10∧(10/10),z(2)=z(t)+z(t)10∧(15/10),z(3)=z(t)+z(t)10∧(20/10),z(4)=z(t)+z(t)10∧(25/10),z(5)=z(t)+z(t)10∧(30/10),z(6)=z(t)+z(t)10∧(35/10),(11)SNR=10log10(PsignalPnoise), where, Psignal and Pniose denote the power of the signal to be measured and the power of the added noise, respectively. From Fig. 9, the performance of SMSDE is better than that of RCMSDE, CMSDE, MSDE, RCMFE, MFE, RCMSE, MSE, and MPE. As the scale factor increases, the curve of SMSDE becomes smoother, and not only is the entropy value more stable, but the resistance to noise disturbance is stronger. Furthermore, RCMSDE outperforms CMSDE and MSDE. The robustness of RCMFE is somewhat better than that of MFE, but the performance of both needs further improvement. RCMSE and MSE are relatively weak in resisting the disturbing effects of noise, and the entropy curve fluctuates significantly, especially for MSE. For MPE, the entropy fluctuates widely and performs poorly under different SNRs.

    3. The proposed SMSDE-based fault diagnosis method

    In this section, to verify the performance of the proposed SMSDE for bearing fault diagnosis, real bearing experimental cases are used for validation. In the experiments, the features of the bearing signals are first extracted by SMSDE, followed by applying SVM for pattern recognition, and the structure framework is shown in Fig. 10. The detailed steps of the proposed method are as follows:

    • (1)

      Signal acquisition. The vibration signals of the machine in different health states are acquired, while the vibration signals are segmented into sample data, each of which has a length of 3500 sample points;

    • (2)

      Feature extraction. The proposed SMSDE is used to extract the fault features of the bearing samples directly, with scale factor τ = 20. That is, the SMSDE is utilized to calculate the sample to obtain the entropy value, and the entropy value of 1–20 scale factors is used as the feature;

    • (3)

      Pattern recognition. The extracted features are randomly divided into training and testing data sets, and the training set is input into the SVM to obtain the training model, followed by inputting the testing set into the training model to identify the various health states of the machine. For the selection of the key parameters (penalty factor C and kernel function G) of the SVM, a grid search technique with three-fold cross-validation is used [58,59].

    4. Experimental verification

    To verify the effectiveness of the proposed SMSDE in mechanical fault diagnosis, three experimental cases are used for validation in this section. Experimental case I comes from our laboratory's mechanical failure test rig, which is used to simulate a variety of fault conditions in rolling bearings. Experimental case II is a bearing test rig from Politecnico di Torino. Additionally, experimental case III comes from the bearing test rig at Case Western Reserve University. Furthermore, for these three experimental cases, not only the working conditions of the bearings are different, but also the sampling frequency of the signals is not the same.

    4.1. Experimental case I

    In this section, the practicality of SMSDE is verified by experimental case I. The dataset for Case I is first introduced, and then the experimental results and analysis are presented.

    4.1.1. Description of experimental data

    The experimental data of Case I are described in this section. The experimental data are collected from the mechanical failure simulation test rig in the laboratory, as shown in Fig. 11. The apparatus consists of the drive motor, motor controller, bearing base, and test bearing, and the vibration acceleration sensor is installed in the vertical direction of the bearing base. The health status of the test bearing is as follows: normal condition, inner ring fault, ball fault, and outer ring fault. The bearing model is MB ER-12 K. Additionally, the fault forms are processed by EDM pitting technology, and the fault diameters of each fault bearing are 1.0 mm, 1.5 mm, and 2.0 mm, respectively. This means that the inner ring fault, ball fault, and outer ring fault have three different defect sizes, respectively. Thus, there are ten bearing categories in total (Table 2).

    During the experiment, the sampling frequency is set to 32,768 Hz and the speed of the bearing is 2200 rpm. Each bearing category contains 120 samples, of which 50% are used for training and the remainder for testing. Additionally, the length of each sample is 3500 sample points. Furthermore, the vibration signals of the 10 bearing categories are shown in Fig. 12. From Fig. 12, it is difficult to distinguish the different health states of the bearing from the waveform of the original signal alone.

    4.1.2. Experimental results and analysis

    The experimental results and analysis of Case I are presented in this section. To illustrate the denoising process of SMSDE, the bearing signal of Case I is used for analysis. SMSDE uses EMD to decompose the signal into 10 IMFs, as shown in Fig. 13. From Fig. 13, the frequency of the signal gradually decreases from IMF1 to IMF10. The correlation coefficient can represent the degree of correlation between the original signal and each IMF. Kurtosis describes the impact response of the bearing, and the larger the kurtosis, the more primary information the IMF contains. From Table 3 and Fig. 14, the correlation coefficients of the first five IMFs are all greater than 0.5, and the kurtosis of the first five IMFs is greater than 5. Thus, the first five IMFs are selected for signal reconstruction, as shown in Fig. 15: compared with the original signal, the reconstructed signal can eliminate meaningless low-frequency components. Therefore, SMSDE can retain the medium and high-frequency components that contain the main information, thus removing the background noise.

    Table 3. Detailed calculation results for the correlation coefficient and kurtosis value of each IMF.

    Empty CellIMF1IMF2IMF3IMF4IMF5IMF6IMF7IMF8IMF9IMF10
    Correlation coefficient0.860.910.780.620.530.390.260.220.180.19
    Kurtosis value9.278.876.935.375.923.242.072.541.811.62

    To verify the effectiveness of the proposed SMSDE, it is applied to the extraction of vibration signal fault features. Additionally, state-of-the-art methods such as RCMSDE, CMSDE, MSDE, RCMFE, MFE, RCMSE, MSE, and MPE have been used for the analysis of experimental data. Nine entropy methods are used to calculate the average of 60 samples for each bearing category signal, and the results are illustrated in Fig. 16. From Fig. 16, the entropy values of the nine methods show a decreasing trend as the scale factor increases. For SMSDE, the entropy curves in each scale factor fluctuate less, and the curves of each category are smoother. The entropy of the normal state of the bearing is then different from that of the fault state, which can indicate the presence of fault. This shows that due to the existence of the fault, the complexity of the normal state signal and the fault state signal are different. Furthermore, the different fault categories are better discriminated and there is no obvious cross-over, which provides sensitive fault features for subsequent fault diagnosis. For the RCMSDE, the entropy curves of a few bearing categories appear to cross and cannot be distinguished from each other. For CMSDE and MSDE, only a few bearing categories can be distinguished, while the discrimination of the remaining categories is not good, and the curves are fluctuating and unstable. The performance of RCMFE, MFE, RCMSE, and MSE is also not ideal, especially in categories OR3 and B3, which almost overlap and cannot be distinguished. In addition, the effect of MPE is even worse, and there is significant overlap between different bearing categories.

    Then, the further to verify the performance of SMSDE in feature extraction, the features extracted by the nine entropy methods in Fig. 16 are input to SVM for fault diagnosis. In each diagnostic trial, there are 120 samples representing each bearing state, giving a total of 1200 samples (120 × 10). Additionally, to reduce the influence of randomness, 20 trials were performed for each method: the diagnostic results are summarized in Table 4. Furthermore, the data points of the test samples are not duplicated in each trial, meaning that each sample is not the same. From Table 4, the mean accuracy of SMSDE is 99.79% with a standard deviation of 0.21, and it has the best diagnostic effect. However, the mean accuracy of RCMSDE, CMSDE, MSDE, RCMFE, MFE, RCMSE, MSE, and MPE is 99.28%, 98.92%, 97.48%, 98.66%, 97.42%, 98.32%, 96.92%, and 96.44%, respectively: the corresponding standard deviations are 0.37, 0.49, 0.71, 0.68, 0.89, 0.72, 0.96, and 1.26, respectively. In addition, detailed results of the accuracy of 20 trials for SMSDE, RCMSDE, CMSDE, RCMFE, and RCMSE are shown in Fig. 17. In terms of computation time, the SMSDE is 769.50 s, while the RCMSDE, CMSDE, RCMFE, and RCMSE are 2151.69 s, 938.37 s, 1722.32 s, and 1199.23 s, respectively. Furthermore, the computation time of RCMSDE and RCMFE is several times that of SMSDE. Therefore, SMSDE not only has good diagnostic performance, but also has high computational efficiency, and it can meet the needs of on-line detection in industrial production.

    To visualize the superiority of the proposed SMSDE, the confusion matrices of SMSDE, RCMSDE, RCMFE, and RCMSE are shown in Fig. 18. From Fig. 18, for the proposed SMSDE, one sample from Category 3 is misclassified as belonging to Category 4 and one from Category 8 is misclassified as belonging to Category 3. However, RCMSDE, RCMFE, and RCMSE have multiple categories that are misclassified, and the number of misclassified samples is 5, 11, and 13, respectively.

    In addition, four general metrics (recall, precision, specificity, and F1 score) were chosen for further study to validate the performance of different methods. These four metrics are defined as follows:(12)Recall=TPTP+FN,Precision=TPTP+FP,Specificity=TNTN+FP,F1score=2×Precision×RecallPrecision+Recall,where TP denotes the number of true positive samples, FN and FP indicate the number of false negative samples and false positive samples, respectively. Similarly, 20 trials were performed for each method to calculate the average and standard deviation. As shown in Table 5, SMSDE can achieve the best performance in each evaluation metric, indicating that it has good generalization ability.

    The further to validate the robustness of the proposed method, the effects of different proportions of training and testing samples on SMSDE, RCMSDE, RCMFE, and RCMSE are evaluated. As per the previous experiment, a total of 600 samples was available, with the proportion of training samples ranging from 10% to 90%. From Fig. 19, with the increase in the proportion of training samples, the diagnostic accuracy of SMSDE, RCMSDE, RCMFE, and RCMSE first increased, then gradually stabilized. Furthermore, the diagnostic performance of SMSDE is better than that of RCMSDE, RCMFE and RCMSE for a smaller number of training samples (10%). This indicates that the proposed SMSDE can still achieve satisfactory diagnostic results when the number of labelled samples is small.

    Furthermore, the influences of scale factors on SMSDE are also analyzed, i.e., the entropy values of 20 scale factors of SMSDE are taken as 20 feature dimensions, and then input into SVM for identification and diagnosis in turn. Meanwhile, 20 trials were carried out and the average accuracy was calculated. From Fig. 20, the accuracy and stability improve significantly as the scale factor becomes larger, followed by a slight fluctuation. Furthermore, when the scale factor is 20, not only is the accuracy maximized, but the stability is optimal. Meanwhile, the computation time increases, by approximately 8 s, but this is deemed acceptable.

    4.2. Experimental case II

    In this section, the practicality of SMSDE is verified by experimental case II. The dataset for Case II is first introduced, and then the experimental results and analysis are presented.

    4.2.1. Description of experimental data

    The experimental data of Case II are described in this section. Case II applied the bearing dataset from the Politecnico di Torino (PDT) [60], and the test rig is shown in Fig. 21. The test rig is used to simulate the bearing fault of the aeroengine, and the health statuses of the test bearing are: normal condition, inner ring fault, and outer ring fault. In addition, the fault diameter of each fault bearing is 450 μm, 250 μm, and 150 μm. Thus, there are a total of seven bearing categories, as listed in Table 6. During the experiment, the sampling frequency is set to 51.2 kHz and the speed of the bearing is 12,000 rpm. Each bearing category contains 120 samples, and the proportion of both training and test samples is 50%. Additionally, the length of each sample is 3500 sample points. Furthermore, the vibration signals of the seven bearing categories are shown in Fig. 22.

    Table 6. Description of the bearing dataset for Case II.

    4.2.2. Experimental results and analysis

    The experimental results and analysis of Case II are presented in this section. The proposed SMSDE is applied to extract fault features from the acquired signals and the output is compared with RCMSDE, CMSDE, MSDE, RCMFE, MFE, RCMSE, MSE, and MPE, respectively. From Fig. 23, for SMSDE, the curves of the normal and faulty states of the bearing are different, which means that the signal complexity of the normal and faulty states differs in the presence of the fault. In addition, the different fault categories are clearly identified, with no significant overlap. Furthermore, once the scale factor exceeds 10, the seven bearing categories can be visually distinguished. This demonstrates that SMSDE can extract the fault features of bearings and can provide sensitive features for subsequent fault diagnosis. For RCMSDE, CMSDE, and MSDE, the entropy value curves of a few bearing categories exhibit severe overlap, resulting in poor discrimination between states. For RCMFE and RCMSE, the entropy curves of most bearing health states overlap, making it more difficult to distinguish different bearing categories, and the effect is sub-optimal. Similarly, for MFE, MSE, and MPE, not only do the entropy curves of each bearing category overlap, but the curves are not smooth, and the ability to distinguish categories is poorer.

    The features extracted by the aforementioned nine methods were then input into the SVM for fault diagnosis, and 20 trials were performed for each method to avoid randomness. In each diagnostic trial, there are 120 samples for each bearing status, giving a total of 840 samples (120 × 7). Furthermore, the data points pertaining to each test sample are not duplicated in each trial. From Table 7, the mean accuracy of the proposed SMSDE is 99.84% with a standard deviation of 0.17, suggesting the best diagnostic effect. In addition, the diagnostic effect of MSDE is poorer than that of SMSDE, RCMSDE, and CMSDE. For RCMFE, MFE, RCMSE, MSE, and MPE, none of them perform well in diagnostic terms. Furthermore, the detailed results of the accuracy of 20 trials for SMSDE, RCMSDE, CMSDE, RCMFE, and RCMSE are shown in Fig. 24: SMSDE also achieves satisfactory results in terms of computation time.

    4.3. Experimental case III

    In this section, the practicality of SMSDE is verified by experimental case III. The dataset for Case III is first introduced, and then the experimental results and analysis are presented.

    4.3.1. Description of experimental data

    The experimental data of Case III are described in this section. The data for Case III were collected from Case Western Reserve University (CWRU)’s bearing test rig [61], which comprises a drive motor, torque transducer, and load motor (Fig. 27). The health statuses of the test bearing are: normal condition, inner ring fault, ball fault, and outer ring fault. The bearing is an SKF 6205 model. Additionally, the fault diameters of each fault bearing are 0.007 in (0.178 mm), 0.014 in (0.356 mm), and 0.028 in (0.711 mm), respectively. Thus, there are ten bearing categories in total (Table 9). Each category contains 120 samples, and the number of both training and test samples is 60. Furthermore, the length of each sample is 3500 sample points. The motor speed is 1750 rpm, and the sampling frequency is 48 kHz. In addition, the vibration signals pertaining to each of the 10 bearing categories are presented in Fig. 28.

    4.3.2. Experimental results and analysis

    The experimental results and analysis of Case III are presented in this section. Akin to Case I, SMSDE is applied to extract fault features from the collected signals and compared with different entropy methods (Fig. 29). Additionally, it can be seen from Cases I and II that MFE, MSE, and MPE are less effective compared with other entropy methods, so they will not be discussed in much more depth herein. From Fig. 29, the entropy curve of SMSDE becomes smoother as the scale factor increases, and not only is the discrimination of each bearing category more significant, but there is also no significant overlap. This means that SMSDE can be used to describe the complexity of bearing vibration signals to good effect. Furthermore, when the scale factor exceeds, it is possible to distinguish visually between the 10 bearing categories. Nevertheless, for RCMSDE, CMSDE, MSDE, RCMFE, and RCMSE, the entropy curves of some bearing classes fluctuate widely and overlap, resulting in poor discrimination.

    The features extracted by the six methods were then input into the SVM for fault diagnosis, 20 trials were conducted for each method, and the results are summarized in Table 10. In each diagnostic trial, 1200 samples (120 × 10) were selected. Furthermore, the data points pertaining to each test sample were not duplicated. From Table 10, the mean accuracy of SMSDE is 99.73% with a standard deviation of 0.28, and it returns the best performance. Additionally, the detailed results of 20 trials for SMSDE, RCMSDE, CMSDE, RCMFE, and RCMSE are shown in Fig. 30. From Table 10 and Fig. 30, SMSDE not only has high accuracy and stability, but also demonstrates satisfactory computational efficiency, and it outperforms the other methods. Furthermore, from the comparison of the confusion matrix in Fig. 31, the result of the fault identification of SMSDE is better than that of RCMSDE.

    5. Conclusions and future work

    In this study, a novel method for signal complexity analysis called SMSDE was proposed and applied to extract sensitive fault features from machinery. For SMSDE, it integrates the merits of IMF reconstruction and the slippage-averaging multiscale approach. Thus, SMSDE not only reduces noise but also mines key signal information, thus extracting sensitive features.

    To verify the effectiveness of SMSDE, it was verified by several experiments. Firstly, the analysis of bearing vibration signals shows that the proposed SMSDE not only describes the complexity of vibration signals more accurately than RCMSDE, CMSDE, MSDE, RCMFE, MFE, RCMSE, MSE, and MPE, but also better distinguishes between different health states. Thus, SMSDE can extract sensitive features of bearing faults. Secondly, the three bearing experimental cases show that SMSDE has good accuracy and robustness in fault diagnosis compared with other entropy methods, which not only have high computational efficiency but can still obtain desirable results under different training sample proportions. Meanwhile, SMSDE can achieve the best performance in four evaluation metrics, which indicates that it has good generalization ability. Additionally, the experimental results of multiple synthesized signals imply that SMSDE has better performance regarding three aspects: data length, entropy stability, and anti-noise interference ability.

    This study also provides a new perspective for fault information extraction of engineering machinery. In future research work, further reduction of SMSDE calculation time will be considered and its effectiveness will be verified in the health monitoring of other engineering machines.
